modern: In the gymnasium, suppose that a man has scratched you with his nails, and by butting against your head has given you a wound. Well, we show no signs of annoyance, nor are we offended, nor do we suspect him afterwards of being a treacherous fellow; and yet we are on our guard against him, though not as an enemy, nor with suspicion, but we quietly get out of his way. Let your behaviour be something like this in all the other parts of life; let us overlook many things in those who are like opponents in the gymnasium. For it is in our power, as I said, to get out of the way, and to have neither suspicion nor hatred.
original: In the gymnastic exercises suppose that a man has torn thee with his nails, and by dashing against thy head has inflicted a wound. Well, we neither show any signs of vexation, nor are we offended, nor do we suspect him afterwards as a treacherous fellow; and yet we are on our guard against him, not however as an enemy, nor yet with suspicion, but we quietly get out of his way. Something like this let thy behavior be in all the other parts of life; let us overlook many things in those who are like antagonists in the gymnasium. For it is in our power, as I said, to get out of the way, and to have no suspicion nor hatred.

explained.summary:
In a training bout, if someone scratches you or butts your head, you don’t take it personally, sulk, or decide they’re treacherous. You just keep an eye on them and step out of the way, without hostility. Marcus wants to treat the rest of life like that.

Many people who knock into you are more like sparring partners than enemies. You can overlook a lot, avoid getting hurt again, and still feel neither suspicion nor hatred.
explained.today: In five-a-side football someone clips your ankle and you shrug it off. Do the same with the driver who cuts you up or the colleague who talks over you: give them a bit more room next time, but don’t build a grudge out of it.
